extraction.name: MathQA
extraction.description: A large-scale dataset of 37,200 math word problems with corresponding lists of multiple-choice options and aligned operation programs. MathQA significantly enhances the AQuA dataset with fully-specified operational programs using a new operation-based representation language covering multiple math domain categories including Geometry, Physics, Probability, Gain-Loss, General, and Other.
extraction.creator: Aida Amini, Saadia Gabriel, Shanchuan Lin, Rik Koncel-Kedziorski, Yejin Choi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi (University of Washington, Allen Institute for AI)
extraction.citeAs: Amini, A., Gabriel, S., Lin, S., Koncel-Kedziorski, R., Choi, Y., & Hajishirzi, H. (2019). MathQA: Towards Interpretable Math Word Problem Solving with Operation-Based Formalisms. arXiv:1905.13319v1 [cs.CL].
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Math word problems were sourced from the AQuA dataset and carefully annotated with formal operation programs using a dynamic crowd-sourcing annotation platform. Problems were first categorized into math domains using term frequencies, and annotators iteratively selected operations and arguments until each problem was solved. An automatic dynamic programming approach was also experimented with but not included due to noise.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Many problems in the AQuA dataset were found to be unsolvable or noisy, including problems with incorrect solutions, near-duplicates, sequence problems, non-numeric problems, and problems requiring brute-force enumeration. These were excluded from the final MathQA dataset.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: The AQuA (AQUA-RAT) dataset by Ling et al. (2017), which contains over 100K GRE- and GMAT-level multiple-choice math word problems expanded from approximately 30,000 seed problems through crowdsourcing.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Annotation expansion was performed by finding closely similar problems using Levenshtein distance with a threshold of 4 words in edit distance, replacing numeric values with generic numbers, and expanding annotations to cover more problems from the AQuA dataset.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems were categorized into math domains using term frequencies. Unsolvable problems were identified and excluded, including: problems with no words, sequence problems, problems requiring options, non-numeric problems, and duplicates. The dataset was randomly split into 80/12/8% training/dev/test sets.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: A dynamic annotation platform was used where annotators were provided with a problem description, a list of operations related to the problem category, and a list of valid arguments. Annotators iteratively selected operations and arguments until the problem was solved. Quality control was enforced through pre-defined test questions and accuracy thresholds. Programs were only accepted if they included numbers from the problem and whose final calculation was close to the correct numeric solution. A validation strategy required at least 2 out of 3 validators to rank the operation program as valid for it to be selected.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Expert evaluation of 500 problems showed 92% of annotations are valid. Agreement between expert validation and crowd-sourcing validation was 87%. Validation accuracy across categories was 94.64%. Annotators who dropped below an accuracy threshold had their previous annotations labeled as untrusted and re-added to the annotation pool.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 validators per annotation (2 out of 3 must agree for acceptance)
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: An automatic dynamic programming approach was experimented with to generate operation programs using numbers in the AQuA rationales, but was not included in the final dataset due to noise (only 61% passed human validation).
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The AQuA dataset contains significant noise including problems with incorrect solutions, near-duplicates with slight changes not reflected in rationales, and problems unsolvable without brute-force. The categorization strategy may be noisy due to use of only one mathematical interpretation for each domain-specific n-gram (e.g., 'square' or 'cube' can refer to geometry or exponential operations).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset omits high-order polynomials and problems where solutions are entirely non-numeric. Sequence problems requiring pattern understanding are currently unsolvable. The representation language does not include all mathematical operations (e.g., factorization). Model performance is still significantly lower than human performance. Problems that can only be solved by brute-force or guessing are excluded.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of neural math word problem solvers. The dataset is intended for use in training deep learning models to solve math word problems through operation program generation. It can also be used to evaluate model interpretability and logical reasoning capabilities.
